desc:
The m x n matrix mat has rows sorted in non-decreasing order. A pick chooses exactly one cell from every row (one column index per row), and its sum is the total of the chosen values. Two picks that use different column indices in some row are different picks, even if their sums are equal, so there are nm picks in total.

Sort the sums of all picks in non-decreasing order and return the k-th one (1-based).

mat = [[1, 3, 11],
       [2, 4, 6]], k = 5
all nine sums: 3, 5, 7, 5, 7, 9, 13, 15, 17
sorted:        3, 5, 5, 7, 7, 9, 13, 15, 17
result = 7
constraints: Every row is sorted in non-decreasing order
hints: There can be 40<sup>40</sup> picks, so you cannot list them. But k is small. Which sums can possibly matter?
Ask the counting question instead: how many picks have sum ≤ S? It grows with S, so you can binary search the smallest S whose count reaches k. You never need the exact count above k.

Count with a depth-first search over rows, choosing columns left to right and stopping a row as soon as the sum can no longer be completed within S (use the sum of every later row's first element as the cheapest completion). Quit the whole search once the count reaches k; the pruning keeps every visited node on a path to a valid pick, so at most about m * k nodes are visited.
editorial: The k-th smallest sum is the smallest S such that at least k picks have sum ≤ S. The number of picks with sum ≤ S does not decrease when S grows, so we can binary search S between the smallest possible sum (every row's first value added up) and the largest one (every row's last value added up).

To test S we count picks with sum ≤ S, but only up to k. Precompute rest[i], the sum of the first elements of rows i..m-1, the cheapest way to finish from row i. In the DFS at row i with budget b, try columns in order; since rows are sorted, stop at the first value v with v + rest[i+1] > b. Every node we enter can be completed into at least one valid pick, so the number of visited nodes is at most m times the number of counted picks, and we abort the search as soon as k picks are found. One probe therefore costs O(m * k) steps.

With about log(m * 5000) ≤ 18 probes the total time is O(m k log(m * maxValue)) and the extra space is O(m) for the recursion. An alternative is to merge the rows one at a time, keeping only the k smallest partial sums with a heap, which costs O(m k log k).
